_comment: Generated by tools/assets/plants.py; the species are defined there. Triangle counts are measured after triangulation.

banana.tells: Ribbon-torn giant blades on a smooth green column.
banana.reference: A pseudostem of rolled sheaths 0.2-0.4 m thick to 3-6 m, with 8-12 blades 2-3 m long and 0.5-0.9 m wide that tear along the lateral veins into ribbons within weeks of opening.
banana.historical: Musa is Asian: POWO gives its native range as tropical and subtropical Asia to the western Pacific, with no American country in it. The defensible claim is '16th century, via the Canaries and the Caribbean'; the usual '1516, Berlanga' is traditional attribution, not fact. No banana of any kind in a pre-contact scene - not background, not thatch, not a wrapping leaf. Substitute `calathea` (Calathea lutea) or a big heliconia; what separates them at a distance is that the native blades stay entire instead of shredding into the banana comb, and that there is no fruit hand or drooping purple bell.

bromeliad_epiphyte.tells: A stiff green urn clamped onto a branch where nothing should grow.
bromeliad_epiphyte.reference: Tank bromeliads sit in branch forks and trunk crotches through the Petén, their rosettes 0.4-1.2 m across holding water between overlapping, often red-flushed strap leaves; they are the commonest large epiphyte on old trees and ruins.
bromeliad_epiphyte.assumed: The water tank is implied by the leaf bases, not modelled.

bromeliad_ground.tells: A fountain of stiff, spine-edged straps with a reddish base and recurved tips.
bromeliad_ground.reference: A. magdalenae forms dense terrestrial rosettes in Petén forest, its spine-edged strap leaves 1-2 m long and 5-10 cm wide, recurving from an upright base; the fibre was worked into cordage. It makes near-impassable thickets.
bromeliad_ground.assumed: Spine geometry is left to the texture; building spines would cost more than the leaf.

calathea.tells: Huge upright paddles with a chalk-white back, standing almost vertically.
calathea.reference: Calathea lutea stands 2-3 m in wet lowland openings, with upright paddle blades 0.5-1.0 m long and 0.3-0.5 m wide on long petioles; the underside carries a waxy white bloom that flashes when the leaf turns. The leaves are the tamale wrapper of the Maya lowlands, so it belongs near any inhabited clearing.

canopy_tree.tells: A dense, dark, rounded crown over a clean grey bole.
canopy_tree.reference: Brosimum alicastrum is the dominant canopy tree of Petén forest, 20-35 m with a straight unbuttressed-to-lightly-buttressed bole and a dense, rounded crown of glossy entire leaves; it grows thickly on Maya ruins, where the Maya may have encouraged it. It is the right default wall of jungle behind a temple.
canopy_tree.assumed: Crown is built as overlapping leaf shells; at 20-40 m only the silhouette carries.

ceiba.tells: The buttresses. Tall sinuous grey walls taller than a person, radiating across the litter, with a spine-studded grey bole rising out of them. At 5-15 m the crown is out of frame: the tree IS its buttresses.
ceiba.reference: 10-30 m is common, 30 modal, 60-70 exceptional, so 35-45 m is the honest emergent and 50 m a hero tree; bole 1.0-3.0 m, use 1.2-2.0 m dbh above the flare. Branches are 'spreading, whorled and almost horizontal' under a thin pagoda crown 25-40 m across; leaves are palmately compound with 5-9 leaflets (usually 5 on mature trees) 0.08-0.16 x 0.02-0.04 m; the trunk carries short sharp prickles. It is the Maya world tree, the axis mundi joining Underworld, earth and sky, so it is the one canopy tree a temple scene must not get wrong.
ceiba.assumed: The buttresses, which are also the thing the player sees: the circulating 12-15 m high / 20 m spread figures trace to popular books, not measurement, and the one measured datum is a 49.7 m BCI tree whose whole buttressed base was 15 m across (about 6-7 m radial). Built here as 5-9 planks about 0.15-0.20 of the tree's height, spreading 3-6 m, 0.3-0.6 m thick at the ground, with surface roots running on across the litter, which is the regionally correct read on Peten karst where roots spread horizontally rather than plunging. Spine size and shedding age, and the leafless months, are also unsourced.

corozo_palm.tells: A shuttlecock: a funnel of near-vertical plumose fronds, wider than it is tall, on a trunk collared with old leaf bases.
corozo_palm.reference: 9-15 m attested (the 20-30 m figures are secondary), with 20-30 fronds that the Flora of Guatemala describes as sometimes 10 m long and 2 m wide, 'plume-like and graceful despite their size'. The trunk is clean below and collared with persistent leaf bases above. Young plants are acaulescent - a giant stemless shuttlecock standing on the floor, and very common. It is 'abundant in the Atlantic lowlands... chiefly at 300 m or lower', which is the Belize cohune ridge; the Maya name is tutz, and the pendent fruiting panicle carries 800-1000 fruits like small coconuts and can pass 45 kg.
corozo_palm.assumed: Frond count is cut to a third of the real 20-30 for the triangle budget and the texture carries the leaflet density the geometry cannot; trunk diameter and leaflet width come from secondary sources only.

cycad.tells: An apparently trunkless, stiff rosette of a handful of very large saw-edged leaflets standing straight out of bare limestone litter: a fern-palm with no stem and far too few leaves.
cycad.reference: The Maya-lowland cycad is Z. prasina, distributed through Belize, Peten, Campeche, Chiapas, Tabasco, Quintana Roo and Yucatan (GBIF: MX 336, BZ 128, GT 14). Z. loddigesii is Tamaulipas to Chiapas and Dioon is montane, so neither belongs. The stem is HYPOGEOUS - subterranean, to 10-15 cm - so there is no trunk to model; that is the commonest mistake in game cycads. 2-3 leaves (range 1-5) 0.5-1.5 m, petiole 0.15-0.50 m and prickled, 3-12 leaflet pairs, largest leaflets 0.20-0.30 x 0.02-0.08 m (about 5:1), serrate on the upper two thirds, with many fine parallel veins and no midrib. It grows on rocky limestone.
cycad.assumed: Cones are omitted; only the foliage is built.

fan_palm.tells: The silver-white underside flashing over a trunk bristling with downward root-spines.
fan_palm.reference: Belize, Peten and Chiapas, to 8 m and often on limestone (GBIF MX 245, BZ 82, GT 34). The leaf is PALMATE, not costapalmate - there is no midrib running out into the blade - with about 44 ribs and 9 divisions a side, cleft almost to the petiole, the blade about 1.0-1.4 m across on a petiole 0.70-1.20 m, green above and rusty-scurfy beneath. The trunk is a very slender pole about 5 cm thick, armed with pungent simple or branched spiny rhizoids pointing downward: the give-and-take.
fan_palm.assumed: Spine length and density are printed nowhere reachable (5-15 cm, dense over the lower 1-3 m, branched into 2-5 points); they are carried by the bark texture. Leaf count per crown.

forest_grass.tells: Thin bamboo-like canes arching out of a gap, with wide flat drooping blades. Never a lawn tuft, and never continuous cover.
forest_grass.reference: Olyra latifolia is a broad-leaved woody grass of Mesoamerican lowland forest, 0.6-4 m but 0.6-1.5 m in deep shade, with woody cane-like culms and distinct nodes, blades 0.10-0.20 m by 0.030-0.060 m (about 3.3:1). It belongs to gaps, treefalls, trail and plaza edges, NOT the deep interior - 14 of 96 Guatemalan records are Peten.

heliconia.tells: Erect, torn, strap-shaped blades in one plane, with a flame-coloured spike.
heliconia.reference: Lowland Heliconia stand 1.5-3 m, with banana-like blades 0.6-1.2 m long and 0.15-0.3 m wide on long sheathing petioles, held steeply erect and tearing along the lateral veins with age; the inflorescence is a zig-zag of red-orange bracts.
heliconia.assumed: Bract geometry is simplified to one zig-zag spike; the bracts' exact count varies.

leaf_litter.tells: Fresh pale leaves standing proud and curled on a dark flat mat, with 1-3 m silver-grey palm frond segments as the only large shapes.
leaf_litter.reference: Litter, not soil, IS the ground surface here: southern Yucatan mature forest drops about 6.2 Mg/ha/yr (Calakmul 5.2-7.1) of which leaves are 84-91%, and litterfall peaks in the dry season with a pulse in late March and early April, so a March scene has the deepest, freshest, most yellow-tan floor. Fallen blades are mesophyll class, 45-182 cm2, so 12-25 cm long and 5-10 cm wide, with a long tail of 3-8 cm Fabaceae leaflets. Whole leaves become fragments in about 2.1 years, and the visible layer is replaced roughly annually. Palm frond segments 1-3 m long weather paler than dicot leaves - straw to silver-grey - and stay recognisable far longer, so they read as the pale shapes on a dark mat.
leaf_litter.assumed: Depth in centimetres, ground-cover percentage and leaf count per patch: no source found. Built as 2-5 cm with 10-20 cm in buttress pockets and against logs, and 90-100% cover under closed canopy.

liana.tells: A leafless grey flat ribbon of wood the width of a hand, hanging clear of everything and twisting through a slow S every metre: a strap, never a cylinder.
liana.reference: The Bauhinia-group liana of this exact setting: Peten, Alta Verapaz and Izabal below 300 m, the most-collected candidate (GBIF MX 700, BZ 83, GT 46), to 18 m long, with bilobate blades 3-8 cm long and about as wide, cordate, 9-nerved, glabrate above and brownish-pilose beneath so the foliage flips fawn-brown in wind, and numerous tendrils. Related Schnella stems are 'flattened and folded, with wings on both sides' when old and round when young, and B. hondurensis stems are 'strongly zigzag, perforated'. In Yucatan the Maya have long used the vine to lash roof frames.
liana.assumed: The ribbon's millimetres are nowhere in print: 60-200 mm wide against 15-40 mm thick (4:1 to 6:1), reversing every 0.6-1.5 m with 60-150 mm of amplitude, free span 3-12 m between crowns. All estimated.

lichen_crust.tells: Value pattern, not texture: a map-like patchwork of pale off-white and cream with irregular dark edges, lighter than the stone, and no free margins anywhere.
lichen_crust.reference: Crustose lichen, not beard lichen: fruticose hanging strands are a cloud-forest signature and are essentially absent at 150-300 m, so a furry green trunk reads as 1500 m and wrecks the altitude. Lowland bark carries flat, paint-like crusts with no free edge - script lichens as black pen-strokes on off-white, Pyrenulaceae as cream-ochre crusts with black dots, Herpothallon as felty white-grey, sometimes rust-orange Trentepohlia algal film. Patches 2-15 cm, merging into mottled sheets 30-80 cm along a trunk, under 1 mm thick.
lichen_crust.assumed: Colony count per patch. Cover figures (50-80% on saplings, 20-40% on big trunks) are scaled down from a Mexican tropical DRY forest study, the only measurement found.

monstera.tells: A short vertical file of sickle blades on long erect petioles, each punched with one or two rows of long oval holes that read as light, not as leaf.
monstera.reference: M. deliciosa is montane here - 450-2620 m, and every georeferenced Guatemalan record is Sacatepequez, Alta Verapaz, Solola or Guatemala, none in Peten, Belize or Yucatan - so the lowland species is M. acuminata (Belize Toledo, 50-1000 m) or M. acacoyaguensis (0-200 m). M. acuminata: internodes 1.0-8.5 cm and 1-3 cm thick, blades 0.35-0.72 x 0.15-0.40 m (1.8-2.3:1), petioles 0.25-0.66 m, and 1-6 (rarely 9) oblong-elliptical holes set between the midrib and the margin, with 6-15 lateral veins a side at 35-60 degrees. M. tuberculata's juvenile shingle phase is 5-10 cm, leathery, pressed flat to the host, and has no holes.
monstera.assumed: Hole placement is procedural along the laterals; real fenestrations are more irregular toward the margin. Climbing height.

moss_patch.tells: A chalky, almost chalk-pale green that is lighter than the stone and bark around it, hugging the bottom metre and the seeping joints only.
moss_patch.reference: Lowland moss is thin creeping weft, not cushion, and it lives in the bottom 1-2 m: trunk bases, buttresses, rotting logs, permanently shaded or seeping limestone. Octoblepharum albidum, the signature pale moss of lowland trunks at about 200 m, makes tufts 0.5-1.5 cm tall of 3-6 mm strap leaves and is described as whitish green - LIGHTER than the bark it sits on, which is what makes it recognisable. Mats run 10-40 cm and 3-10 mm thick on bark, up to 1-2 m and 10-25 mm thick on wet limestone. Wetting darkens it and rotates the hue toward green; it does not simply darken.
moss_patch.assumed: Patch counts, and cover on shaded limestone (30-60% on permanently damp shaded rock, under 5% on sun-struck or dusty rock) are estimates: no source found.

nest_fern.tells: A smooth green funnel of undivided fronds: a fern with no divisions at all.
nest_fern.reference: Asplenium serratum, the neotropical bird's-nest fern, holds a funnel of simple undivided strap fronds 0.4-1.2 m long with wavy, finely toothed margins, on trunks and in branch crotches where litter collects in the funnel.

pacaya_palm.tells: A green bamboo-like cane with prominent rings and a loose crown of few broad leaflets.
pacaya_palm.reference: Chamaedorea tepejilote is the common understory palm of Petén and Chiapas wet forest: a solitary ringed cane 2-6 cm thick to about 3-5 m, with 4-8 pinnate leaves 0.6-1.2 m long whose leaflets are broad and few. Its male inflorescence is eaten; it grows where the canopy is closed.

philodendron.tells: A near-black-green hand of narrow finger-lobes up to a metre across, off a thick green stem glued flat to the trunk, with pale cord roots dropping free below.
philodendron.reference: Croat's revision gives P. radiatum blades 0.27-1.01 m long by 0.25-0.90 m wide - length to width about 1.1-1.2:1, so nearly as wide as long, never a long quad - on petioles 0.28-1.08 m, with internodes 3-12 cm and 1-8 cm thick, incised to within 1-8 cm of the midrib, about 7-13 divisions a side, each pinna 3.0-4.5 cm wide. It climbs 3-12 m with the stem flat against the bark. Aroids and ferns, not grasses, dominate this forest's herb layer (13 of 23 understory species at Los Tuxtlas were aroids).
philodendron.assumed: Leaf count per rosette and climbing height.

root_curtain.tells: Dead-straight pale strands, nothing growing on them, hanging free of the trunk.
root_curtain.reference: Aerial roots hang in curtains from fig crowns and from aroids on high branches, unbranched, 5-25 mm thick, pale brown and hairless, thickening where they reach the ground and root.

shade_grass.tells: Broad near-horizontal blades sitting low and flat like scattered plates, widely separated, with brown litter between them.
shade_grass.reference: The signature grass of closed lowland forest, and nothing like turf: a culm 0.30-1.00 m with a stem only about 3 mm thick, mostly hidden by its own blades, each 0.15-0.30 m long and 0.03-0.08 m wide (about 4:1) on a false petiole 0.05-0.07 m. The blades are RESUPINATE - the false petiole twists so the morphological underside faces up - and sit near-horizontal, like scattered plates. There is no grass floor in this forest: at Los Tuxtlas the lowland herb layer was 23 species dominated by aroids (13) and ferns (4), with no grasses or sedges among the dominants, so plant this as isolated accents on brown litter, never as cover.
shade_grass.assumed: Blade angle, tuft count, and herbaceous cover (5-15% under intact canopy, 40-80% only in treefall gaps): no source gives a percentage.

spikemoss.tells: A flat, fern-like carpet, far finer than any seedling, hugging the ground.
spikemoss.reference: Selaginella forms low, frondose mats 5-30 cm high over deep-shade forest floor and damp stone in the Petén, with flat, finely divided sprays held almost horizontally, often with a blue-green iridescence in low light.

spiny_palm.tells: A pencil-thin black-spined pole under a huge feather that flashes blue-grey when it turns.
spiny_palm.reference: This replaces the stilt palm, which does not belong: GBIF holds 1,910 preserved records of Socratea exorrhiza with a northern limit in Nicaragua and ZERO from Mexico, Guatemala, Belize or Honduras, and Iriartea the same. There is no cone-of-stilt-roots palm in the Peten, and a walking palm here is a visible error. Astrocaryum mexicanum is the palm that is actually there (GBIF MX 231, BZ 54, HN 34, GT 33; the Flora of Guatemala calls it common and often abundant below 400 m): 1.5-5.5 m on a plain slender trunk only 2.5-4.5 cm thick, armed with very numerous spreading stout black spines 3-5 cm long, carrying 4-8 pinnate leaves around a metre long whose few, very long broad segments are glaucous blue-grey beneath. No stilt roots and no crownshaft.
spiny_palm.assumed: Leaf count per crown, segment width, and spine density (about 10-25 per 10 cm of trunk); the spines are carried by the bark texture, not built.

strangler_fig.tells: The vertical seam-and-weld texture of the root column: parallel woody straps running straight down, fusing at irregular crossings, daylight through the gaps, wrapped around a straight dead trunk of completely different bark.
strangler_fig.reference: F. obtusifolia, not F. aurea: the Flora of Guatemala knew Guatemalan F. aurea only from one Sacatepequez collection at about 1500 m, while F. obtusifolia is described as 'usually a conspicuous strangler, especially when juvenile', reaches 40 m, and carries entire glossy leaves 0.15-0.25 x 0.06-0.12 m clustered at the branch ends with 8-11 vein pairs and green globose figs 1.5-3 cm. F. involuta is the Peten-and-Izabal alternative. The aerial roots reach the ground and form a shell-like trunk around the host; the local name is matapalo. This is the tree that grows out of Maya ruins, so it earns its place on an overgrown temple more than any other plant in the library.
strangler_fig.assumed: All the lattice geometry: strand diameter 20-150 mm at head height tapering to 8-25 mm, spacing 100-400 mm where open and fused to a sheet below, sheathing the lower 3-8 m. No source gives any of it, nor how long strangling takes - do not put a duration in player-facing text.

tillandsia.tells: A silver-grey spiky ball on a bare branch, much paler than every leaf around it.
tillandsia.reference: Atmospheric Tillandsia clump on thin branches and on exposed stone, their narrow channelled leaves covered in silver trichomes that make them read grey-green and matt even in rain; clumps run 10-50 cm.

tree_fern.tells: A slender, bare, almost-black pole with no dead-frond skirt, carrying one flat shuttlecock of lace-fine fronds wider than the plant is tall.
tree_fern.reference: The lowland Maya tree fern, not the montane one: GBIF holds 181 Guatemalan and 143 Belizean records of S. myosuroides, with hard Peten records at 233 m (San Luis) and Cockscomb Basin at 100 m, while Alsophila cuspidata is montane here (all three Guatemalan records Alta Verapaz, 956 m). Trunk 6-12 cm across, 3-7 m (typically 4-5); 8-15 bipinnate fronds 1.5-4 m (a measured frond 2.35 x 1.04 m); crown 3-4 m, wider than the plant is tall. Only 10 of 2,528 Guatemalan Cyatheaceae records are Peten, so place it in ravines, streamsides and damp limestone sinks, never on dry karst upland.
tree_fern.assumed: Frond count per crown, and the juvenile rosette size. The second and third orders of division are painted into the leaf texture instead of built, which is what keeps a specimen near 1 k triangles.
